items.prompt: A target-sum solver uses only positive candidate values. When is pruning by remainingTarget < 0 sound?

options.text: When every future choice is positive, so the remaining target can only decrease further.
For arbitrary positive and negative candidates.
Only because the candidates are sorted.
Only after a complete path is built.

feedback.reason: Sound pruning requires a proof that no future choice can repair the violated condition.

blocks.text: Overshoot is permanent only under positive choices

Let remainingTarget equal target minus the sum already chosen. If it is negative, the branch has overshot the exact target. Choosing a future value x > 0 changes it to remainingTarget - x, which is even smaller.

Therefore no sequence of allowed future choices can return the value to zero, and the branch is impossible. Sorting may help encounter overshoot sooner, but positivity—not order—is the fact that proves irreversibility.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: A later negative or compensating value could restore feasibility. Sorting alone does not establish monotonic sum behavior. The point of pruning is to reject impossible partial states early.

blocks.title: Monotonicity test
blocks.text: Prune an overshoot only when every legal continuation moves the tracked quantity farther from feasibility.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_numbers: A later negative or compensating value could restore feasibility.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_sorted: Sorting alone does not establish monotonic sum behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_at_leaf: The point of pruning is to reject impossible partial states early.

items.prompt: Why is the same remainingTarget < 0 prune unsafe when negative candidates are allowed?

options.text: A later negative value can increase the remaining target back toward zero.
Negative values cannot be compared.
Recursion cannot process negative values.
Negative values prevent sorting.

feedback.reason: The monotonicity assumption behind the prune no longer holds.

blocks.text: A negative candidate can reverse an overshoot

With remainingTarget = target - chosenSum, choosing x updates the value to remainingTarget - x. When x is negative, subtracting it increases remainingTarget and can move a negative value back toward zero.

For example, remainingTarget = -3 can be repaired by choosing -3: -3 - (-3) = 0. The prune fails because its required one-directional movement is absent, not because negative numbers are incomparable, unsortable, or incompatible with recursion.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: They can; the issue is reversibility of the sum condition. Recursion is not restricted by sign. Negative values can be sorted.

blocks.title: Counterexample rule
blocks.text: One legal continuation that repairs the condition is enough to invalidate a pruning rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_values_uncomparable: They can; the issue is reversibility of the sum condition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_forbidden: Recursion processes state transitions independently of numeric sign; the problem is the invalid impossibility proof, not the control-flow mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_fails: Negative values have a normal numeric order and can be sorted; sorting does not prevent a later negative choice from repairing the overshoot.

items.prompt: A k-combination solver has chosen c values and has r candidate positions left. Which condition proves completion is impossible?
constraints: Each remaining candidate position can fill at most one slot.

options.text: r < k - c.
r = k - c.
c < k.

feedback.reason: A branch cannot fill more required slots than the number of candidates still available.

blocks.text: Compare remaining demand with maximum supply
A k-combination with c chosen values still needs k - c slots. Under the stated no-reuse model, r remaining candidate positions can supply at most r additional values.

If r < k - c, even choosing every remaining position leaves the combination short, so completion is impossible. Equality is still feasible: r = k - c means every remaining candidate may have to be chosen.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: That means exactly enough candidates remain and may force a valid continuation. Most nonterminal states satisfy this and still can complete. Having candidates remaining does not prove impossibility.

blocks.title: Capacity inequality
blocks.text: Prune when maximum legal supply is strictly smaller than remaining demand.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.r_equals_needed: That means exactly enough candidates remain and may force a valid continuation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.c_less_k: Most nonterminal states satisfy this and still can complete.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.r_positive: A positive r means at least one candidate remains; it provides supply and does not prove that the remaining demand is impossible.

items.prompt: A partial assignment violates a mandatory constraint, and assigning more variables cannot repair that violation. What is the correct action?

options.text: Prune the branch immediately.
Continue until every variable is assigned.
Record the partial assignment as a result.
Remove all sibling branches as well.

feedback.reason: A hereditary constraint violation makes every descendant invalid.

blocks.text: Irreparable violations propagate to every descendant

Every descendant extends the current partial assignment; it does not rewrite choices already fixed in the prefix. The prompt explicitly states that no later assignment can repair the mandatory violation.

Because every full solution must satisfy the constraint, every descendant of this node is invalid. Returning immediately removes only this subtree; siblings begin from different choices and may remain valid.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: No completion can remove an already mandatory violation unless the state model says it is reversible. It is neither complete nor valid. The violation is local to the current branch.

blocks.title: Repairability boundary
blocks.text: A violated partial constraint justifies pruning only when extension cannot restore validity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.continue_all_depths: No completion can remove an already mandatory violation unless the state model says it is reversible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_partial: The assignment is incomplete and already violates a mandatory result condition, so it cannot be emitted as a valid solution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.delete_siblings: The proof concerns descendants that share this violating prefix; siblings choose a different transition and are not covered by it.

items.prompt: A palindrome-partition solver considers a segment that is not a palindrome. Why can that candidate be skipped?

options.text: Every result segment must be a palindrome, and later boundaries cannot change the chosen segment.
Long segments are always invalid.
The branch would probably be slow.
Every repeated segment is invalid.

feedback.reason: Once a boundary fixes the next segment, its validity is permanent within that branch.

blocks.text: A fixed invalid segment cannot be repaired by its suffix
Choosing an exclusive end fixes the next segment [start, end). Every completion of this branch retains that exact segment and only partitions the suffix beginning at end.

If the fixed segment is not a palindrome, every descendant contains an invalid result component. Later boundaries can change only later segments, so skipping this candidate preserves every valid partition.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Length does not determine palindromicity. Expected cost is not a correctness proof. Repetition is not the relevant contract.

blocks.title: Fixed-prefix rule
blocks.text: Reject a candidate when it permanently inserts an invalid component into every possible completion.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.segment_long: Palindromes may be arbitrarily long; length alone does not determine whether the segment reads the same forward and backward.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.branch_slow: Expected runtime may influence traversal order, but it does not prove that the branch lacks a valid partition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_segment: The contract requires palindromic segments, not unique segment values; repetition can be valid unless separately forbidden.

items.prompt: Which statement describes branch ordering rather than pruning?

options.text: Try candidates likely to succeed before other still-legal candidates.
Do not recurse into a state proven unable to complete.
Reject a segment that violates the mandatory predicate.
Stop when too few candidates remain to fill required slots.

feedback.reason: Ordering changes traversal priority but retains every legal branch unless the result contract short-circuits after success.

blocks.text: Ordering postpones branches; pruning removes them

Trying promising candidates first changes only the sequence of exploration. All still-legal candidates remain available, so collect-all output is unchanged; a find-one solver may simply reach its first success earlier.

The other statements omit a subtree: one is proven unable to complete, one violates a mandatory segment predicate, and one lacks enough remaining capacity. Each is pruning or immediate legality filtering backed by impossibility.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: A useful diagnostic is to ask whether the candidate remains scheduled for later. If yes, the rule orders branches; if no, it must prove the omitted subtree cannot matter under the result contract.

blocks.title: Removal test
blocks.text: Priority needs a heuristic; permanent omission needs a correctness proof.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.remove_impossible: The proven-impossible subtree is permanently omitted, which is the defining effect of pruning.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_invalid_segment: The mandatory predicate proves the candidate illegal, so its subtree is filtered out rather than merely delayed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.capacity_bound: Insufficient capacity proves that no descendant can reach the required size, so the entire branch is removed.

items.prompt: A developer prunes a branch because its current score is worse than the best complete score, but future choices may improve the score. What is missing?

options.text: A proven bound showing that no completion of the branch can beat the best result.
A deeper recursion limit.
A sorted candidate list.
A set of previously returned outputs.

feedback.reason: Optimization pruning needs a lower or upper bound on the best possible completion of the partial state.

blocks.text: Compare the incumbent with the branch's best possible completion

A partial score describes work completed so far, not the best score reachable after the remaining decisions. If future choices can improve it, being worse than the current complete incumbent is not yet proof of loss.

For minimization, derive a lower bound on the final score attainable below the branch; prune only if that lower bound cannot beat the incumbent. For maximization, use an upper bound. The bound must be optimistic for the branch so it covers every completion.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Depth does not justify the prune. Sorting alone provides no optimization bound. Output deduplication does not prove optimality.

blocks.title: Branch-and-bound rule
blocks.text: Compare the incumbent with an admissible bound on the best descendant, never with the unfinished score alone.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.more_recursion: A deeper limit explores more states but provides no proof that the current subtree cannot beat the incumbent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting: Candidate order may expose good incumbents earlier, but sorting alone does not bound the best score any descendant can achieve.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_set: Deduplicating completed outputs prevents repeats; it does not establish an upper or lower bound on unfinished assignments.

items.prompt: A grid path still needs L characters, and a proven upper bound shows that fewer than L unused cells are reachable from the current state. What does this establish?

options.text: The branch cannot complete the target and may be pruned.
The remaining path is guaranteed to exist.
No starting position can ever succeed.
Visited state no longer needs restoration.

feedback.reason: A completion requiring more resources than the branch can possibly supply is impossible.

blocks.text: The reachable-cell bound is an upper bound on supply
The path needs one unused reachable cell for each of its L remaining characters. The stated bound proves that the branch can supply at most R cells with R < L.

Even if every reachable cell matched the needed symbols, the route would run out of cells before consuming the target. This proves failure only for the current state. It does not rule out another starting cell or remove the need to undo this branch's visited marks.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Insufficient capacity proves failure, not success. The bound applies to the current branch. Restoration is still needed before returning to the parent.

blocks.title: Bound direction
blocks.text: To prove insufficient supply, use a correct upper bound on what the branch can still reach; an underestimate is unsafe.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.guaranteed_success: The branch has fewer reachable cells than required characters, so even perfect symbol matches cannot produce a complete path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global_failure: The reachability calculation is rooted in the current path state; another start or sibling may have a different reachable region.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.undo_optional: Restoration is still needed before returning to the parent.

items.prompt: Which are sound pruning reasons? Select all that apply.

options.text: A mandatory constraint is already irreversibly violated.
Too few candidates remain to fill required slots.
A positive-only sum branch has already exceeded the target.
The branch looks less promising than its siblings without a proof.

feedback.reason: Sound pruning follows from a proven impossibility condition.

blocks.text: Three independent proofs of impossibility

items: An irreversibly broken mandatory constraint remains broken in every descendant.
Fewer remaining candidates than required slots makes completion exceed maximum capacity.
After a positive-only sum exceeds an exact target, every future positive choice increases the sum further.

blocks.text: Each accepted reason quantifies over every legal continuation. Merely looking less promising compares preferences among siblings and may guide their order, but it gives no impossibility proof.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: A less promising branch may still contain the only valid solution. Without a monotonic condition, capacity bound, or hereditary violation, removing it makes exhaustive search incomplete.

blocks.title: Quantifier test
blocks.text: A safe prune proves that every legal continuation fails, not merely that one likely continuation does.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.looks_unpromising: A heuristic preference can rank this branch later, but without proof it may still contain a valid result and cannot be omitted.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.mandatory_constraint_broken: Because the violation is irreversible and mandatory, every descendant retains an invalid prefix.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.insufficient_candidates: The branch's maximum remaining supply is smaller than its unfilled demand, so no descendant can reach the required size.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.positive_overshoot: With only positive future choices, the current sum moves strictly farther above the exact target.

items.prompt: Which proposed pruning rules are unsafe without additional assumptions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prune target-sum states whenever the current sum exceeds target, even though negative values remain.
Prune an optimization branch because its current partial score is worse, without a completion bound.
Prune every partition segment longer than three when no length constraint exists.
Prune a branch whose prefix already violates a hereditary validity constraint.

feedback.reason: A pruning rule must be tied to explicit monotonicity, capacity, or hereditary constraints.

blocks.text: Identify the missing assumption in each proposed rule

items: Overshoot with negative values is reversible because a later negative choice can reduce the sum.
A worse partial optimization score can improve unless an admissible completion bound rules that out.
A length-three cutoff is invented when the result contract declares no such segment limit.

blocks.text: By contrast, the fourth option explicitly states a hereditary validity constraint. Extension preserves that invalid prefix, so every descendant fails and pruning is sound.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The invalid-prefix option is not one of the unsafe rules: “hereditary” means the violation persists under every extension, which is exactly the required impossibility proof.

blocks.title: Assumption audit
blocks.text: For every prune, name the contract fact that prevents any future choice from repairing the branch.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.invalid_prefix: This rule is sound under the stated hereditary constraint: every extension retains the invalid prefix, so no descendant can satisfy the result contract.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.overshoot_with_negatives: A remaining negative value may lower the accumulated sum back to the target, so current overshoot is not irreversible.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.worse_partial_score: Future decisions may improve the score; pruning requires a bound on the best possible completion, not the partial score alone.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.long_segment: With no contract-defined length limit, a segment longer than three may be valid and cannot be removed by an invented cutoff.

items.prompt: Which facts can support a sound remaining-capacity bound? Select all that apply.

options.text: The number of choices still required.
The number of legal candidates still available.
Whether candidates may be reused.
How many recursive calls have already occurred.

feedback.reason: Capacity pruning compares required future work with the maximum legal supply.

blocks.text: Capacity is demand versus maximum legal supply

items: Remaining slots measure how many additional choices completion demands.
Remaining legal candidates measure the currently available supply.
The reuse rule determines whether one candidate can supply one slot or multiple future slots.

blocks.text: A sound bound uses all applicable facts to compute an upper bound on supply. For no-reuse combinations, r candidates supply at most r slots; with allowed reuse, that same count may not cap future selections.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The number of calls already executed records search history, not how many legal choices the current state can still make. It cannot prove insufficient capacity.

blocks.title: Capacity formula
blocks.text: Prune only when a contract-aware upper bound on supply is smaller than remaining demand.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global_call_count: Call count measures past exploration and is unrelated to the current branch's remaining legal supply or required slots.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.remaining_slots: This is the exact future demand that a completed result must still satisfy.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.remaining_candidates: After legality filtering, this contributes to the maximum supply the current branch can draw from.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.candidate_reuse_rule: Reuse determines whether each candidate can be consumed once or can fill multiple future slots, changing the supply bound.

items.prompt: Which grid conditions can justify pruning the current path? Select all that apply.

options.text: The current cell does not match the required target symbol.
The current cell is already used by the path when reuse is forbidden.
The coordinates are outside the grid.
The preferred neighbor is not tried first.

feedback.reason: These checks reject states that violate immediate legality.

blocks.text: Reject an illegal grid state before expanding neighbors

items: An out-of-bounds coordinate identifies no grid cell and cannot continue the path.
A cell already on the current path violates the stated no-reuse rule.
A cell whose symbol mismatches the next target position cannot represent the required prefix.

blocks.text: Each condition makes the current state immediately illegal, so exploring descendants cannot repair it. Neighbor ordering merely chooses which legal move is tried first and does not change the legal set.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Traversal order does not make the branch impossible.

blocks.title: Grid legality rule
blocks.text: Geometry, path membership, and target progress decide legality; traversal preference decides only order.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.neighbor_order: Traversal order does not make the branch impossible.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.current_mismatch: This branch cannot represent the target prefix.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.cell_reused: The move violates the path contract.

items.prompt: Arrange the process for designing a pruning rule.

elements.text: State the partial condition to be tested.
Prove that every completion from that condition violates the result contract.
Implement the proven condition before branch expansion.
Challenge the proof with counterexamples and boundary cases.

feedback.reason: Pruning begins with a semantic proof, not with code or performance intuition.

blocks.text: Proof and falsification precede optimization code

items: State a predicate over the partial state precisely enough to evaluate it.
Prove that every legal completion from a state satisfying that predicate violates the result contract.
Challenge the proof with repair attempts, equality boundaries, and the smallest counterexamples.
Only after the proof survives, implement the check before expanding the impossible branch.

blocks.text: This order prevents performance intuition from becoming an unchecked correctness rule. Boundary tests can show that a strict comparison should be inclusive, or that an unstated negative value repairs an apparent overshoot.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: Implementing before attempted falsification makes the code appear authoritative even when the predicate is too strong. Testing after implementation may find the defect, but it is not the correct design dependency.

blocks.title: Design rule
blocks.text: Specify, prove, try to disprove, then implement.

items.prompt: Arrange the remaining-slot capacity check for k-combination generation.

elements.text: Compute how many candidate indices remain.
If available < needed, return from the branch.

feedback.reason: The branch is expanded only when its remaining candidate capacity can satisfy the completion size.

blocks.text: Compute demand and supply before expanding

items: Compute needed = k - path.length, the number of unfilled combination slots.
Compute available, the number of legal candidate indices remaining under the no-reuse boundary.
If available < needed, return because maximum supply cannot meet demand.
Otherwise, enumerate legal next candidates; equality is feasible and must not be pruned.

blocks.text: Both quantities must describe the same state and candidate policy. Comparing before computing them uses stale data; enumerating before the comparison performs work inside a subtree already proven impossible.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Compute needed = k - path.length. Then Compute how many candidate indices remain. Then If available < needed, return from the branch. Then Otherwise enumerate legal next candidates. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Boundary rule
blocks.text: Prune on available < needed, not on equality.

items.prompt: A backtracking tree has branching factor b and depth d. Sound pruning removes many branches on typical inputs but no reduction is guaranteed in the worst case. Select the worst-case visited-node bound and recursion depth.
constraints: Some inputs may satisfy no pruning condition until the leaves.

feedback.reason: Pruning may improve actual exploration without changing the formal worst-case class.

blocks.text: Worst case includes inputs where pruning never fires
At level i, a full b-ary tree has at most b^i nodes. Summing levels 0 through d gives (b^(d+1) - 1)/(b - 1), which is O(b^d) for the stated b >= 2.
The prompt guarantees no reduction on every input, so a worst-case input may keep all nodes feasible until the leaves. Pruning may improve typical work but cannot lower this guaranteed class.

Depth-first search holds one root-to-current path at a time. That path contains at most d edges, or d + 1 frames depending on convention, so recursion depth is O(d), independent of the total number of visited nodes.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: O(bd) adds width and depth rather than multiplying branching across levels. O(d^b) swaps the roles of base and exponent. O(b^d) visited nodes do not imply O(b^d) simultaneous stack depth.

blocks.title: Worst-case rule
blocks.text: A pruning optimization changes worst-case complexity only if the prune is guaranteed to remove branches on every valid input.

items.prompt: A subset search makes an include-or-exclude choice for each of n values. Positive-only target pruning may reduce actual work, but select the standard worst-case leaves and recursion depth.
constraints: A branch can make two choices at each input position.
No pruning reduction is guaranteed for every input.

feedback.reason: The binary decision tree has up to 2^n leaves, while one active path contains n decisions.

blocks.text: One binary decision per value

For each of n positions, the solver chooses include or exclude. When pruning does not fire, the independent choices multiply to 2 × 2 × ... × 2 = 2^n complete decision sequences, so the leaf bound is O(2^n).

Positive-only target pruning may cut overshooting branches on some instances, but the prompt explicitly allows inputs for which no guaranteed reduction occurs. Those inputs still realize the binary tree.
A single active root-to-leaf chain decides one input value per level, so it contains n decisions and has O(n) recursion depth. Tree width and live stack depth are different dimensions.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: O(n!) belongs to ordering n distinct values, not binary membership choices. O(2^n) depth confuses all leaves with one active route.

blocks.title: Decision-tree rule
blocks.text: Multiply alternatives across levels for leaves; count levels along one route for recursion depth.

items.prompt: An n-variable assignment solver tries unused values and uses conflict pruning. If every partial assignment remains conflict-free until full depth, select the number of complete branches and recursion depth.
constraints: Each of n distinct values is used exactly once.

feedback.reason: When pruning finds no conflict, the solver still enumerates every permutation-like assignment.

blocks.text: No conflicts means all permutations survive

The first variable can receive any of n distinct values, the second any of n - 1 unused values, and so on. If conflict pruning never rejects a prefix, complete branches number n × (n - 1) × ... × 1 = n!.

The branch factor shrinks because used values are unavailable, not because pruning succeeds. The stated input keeps every partial assignment conflict-free, so the solver cannot omit any permutation-like branch.
Each level assigns one variable, so a complete route has n choices and O(n) recursion depth. The factorial number of complete routes exists across the tree, not simultaneously on the stack.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: O(n^n) would allow reuse of every value at every level, contradicting the unused-value rule. O(2^n) models include/exclude subsets, not one-to-one assignments.

blocks.title: Permutation rule
blocks.text: Conflict pruning helps only where conflicts occur; otherwise the unused-value tree retains n! leaves.

items.prompt: A collect-all pruned solver returns s valid solutions, each of length d. Select the tight asymptotic output work and output space required even if all invalid branches are pruned perfectly.
constraints: Every valid solution must be materialized independently.

feedback.reason: Pruning can remove invalid search work but cannot avoid producing required valid outputs.

blocks.text: Required output imposes an unavoidable cost
The result contains s independently materialized solutions, and each contains d elements. Merely writing those elements performs s × d operations, so output work is Θ(sd).
The stored collection also holds s × d elements, giving Θ(sd) output space. This excludes auxiliary recursion state and describes only the required returned representation.

Perfect pruning can eliminate every invalid branch but cannot compress or omit valid solutions when the contract requires each one independently. Therefore neither output dimension can be O(s), O(d), or O(1) when both s and d grow.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: Search work and output work are separate: pruning attacks the former, while the result contract fixes the latter. A streaming contract could reduce retained output space, but the prompt explicitly requires materialization.

blocks.title: Output lower bound
blocks.text: When s objects of size d must be returned independently, Θ(sd) work and storage are unavoidable.
